commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether documenting a model's purpose, training data, limitations, and evaluation, followed by governance review, changes approval decisions or patient outcomes. Support for the practice rests on 25 endorsing sources, including one state statute, several frameworks, and multiple expert commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The endorsements are frameworks, guidance, and commentaries that express consensus but do not measure effects. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion alone does not establish certainty about whether pre-approval documentation review improves decisions.

CHAI playbooks direct organizations to make model card completion a mandatory approval step, and NIST AI 600-1 asks deployers to document how pre-trained models were adapted. The cited Utah HB 452 text addresses disclosure of AI use to chatbot users rather than internal model documentation, so it offers limited support for this specific recommendation.

The HEAAL framework asks teams to document the rationale for chosen fairness metrics, which would place subgroup performance in front of reviewers. No supplied study examines whether such documentation leads governance bodies to detect or act on performance gaps affecting underserved patients.

CHAI frames documentation as a required workflow step for internally developed AI, which implies staff time from developers and reviewers. No supplied study reports the cost, staffing demand, or review time required, so leaders cannot estimate burden at scale from this evidence.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare approval decisions, time to detection of model limitations, and downstream safety events between AI tools reviewed with standardized documentation (such as model cards) and tools approved without it. Such studies should also measure documentation completeness, reviewer comprehension, and the staff hours the process consumes.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether documentation review surfaces limitations relevant to these groups remains unknown and would depend on whether subgroup data are reported in the documentation itself.
